title: GMAT Focus Data Insights Practice Test 17
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt:
Recycling rates and the cost of the service in five council areas:

Ashwell: 54% recycled, GBP 86.00 a household
Barmouth: 41% recycled, GBP 58.00 a household
Corfield: 62% recycled, GBP 112.00 a household
Dunthorpe: 48% recycled, GBP 64.00 a household
Elmsworth: 58% recycled, GBP 97.00 a household

Which council gets the most recycling for each pound it spends?
questions.explanation: Percentage points per pound spent: Ashwell 0.628, Barmouth 0.707, Corfield 0.554, Dunthorpe 0.750, Elmsworth 0.598. Dunthorpe is best value at 0.750. Corfield recycles the most at 62% but spends GBP 112.00 a household to do it — the highest rate and the worst value in the same column.

questions.prompt:
Annual figures:

2019: 412
2020: 375
2021: 470
2022: 501
2023: 434
2024: 455

In which year was the figure furthest above the six-year mean?
options: E. Every year was above the mean
questions.explanation: The six-year mean is 441.17. Distances from it: 2019 -29.17, 2020 -66.17, 2021 +28.83, 2022 +59.83, 2023 -7.17, 2024 +13.83. 2022 stands 59.83 above it, more than any other year. 2020 is further from the mean in absolute terms, at 66.17, but it lies below it.

questions.prompt:
Every respondent falls into exactly one of these four groups, as a percentage of all respondents:

Under 40 and satisfied: 28%
Under 40 and dissatisfied: 12%
40 or over and satisfied: 35%
40 or over and dissatisfied: 25%

What percentage of respondents aged 40 or over were satisfied?
questions.explanation: 60% of all respondents are aged 40 or over, and 35% are both in that age group and satisfied. The question asks for a share of that age group, not of everybody: 35 / 60 = 58.33%. 35.0% is the figure the table gives directly, but it is measured against all respondents.

questions.prompt:
Two sets of eight readings:

Set A: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 30
Set B: 10, 11, 12, 13, 27, 28, 29, 30

Which statement about the two sets is accurate?
options: A. Set A has the larger range
B. The two sets have the same interquartile range
C. The two sets share a range, but B's interquartile range is more than twice A's
D. Set B has the smaller interquartile range
E. Set A is more spread out through its middle than set B
questions.explanation: Both sets run from 10 to 30, so both have a range of 20 and the range cannot tell them apart. The quartiles can: A has an interquartile range of 8 against B's 17, because B's readings sit in two clumps at the ends while A's are spread evenly. Two sets can share a range and still be shaped quite differently.

questions.prompt:
Electricity costs GBP 22.00 a quarter as a standing charge, plus 18p a unit for the first 400 units and 11p a unit after that.

Select the bill for 350 units AND the bill for 900 units.
questions.explanation: 350 units stay inside the first band: GBP 22.00 + 350 × 18p = GBP 85.00. 900 units use 400 at the higher rate and 500 at the lower: GBP 22.00 + GBP 72.00 + GBP 55.00 = GBP 149.00. Charging all 900 units at the higher rate gives GBP 184.00, and forgetting the standing charge on the small bill gives GBP 63.00.

questions.prompt:
A machine is sold for GBP 8,400.00, at a loss of 20% on what was paid for it.

Select the price originally paid AND the loss in pounds.
questions.explanation: The sale price is 80% of what was paid, so the original price is GBP 8,400.00 / 0.8 = GBP 10,500.00 and the loss GBP 2,100.00. Adding 20% to the sale price gives GBP 10,080.00, because 20% of the smaller figure is less than 20% of the larger one — the loss is measured against what was paid, not against what it fetched.

questions.prompt:
Two depots last month:

Depot One: 4,200 deliveries, 96% on time
Depot Two: 900 deliveries, 88% on time

Select the depot with the better on-time record AND the depot with fewer late deliveries.
options: A. Depot One on both measures
B. Depot Two on both measures
C. Depot Two on the on-time record; Depot One on late deliveries
D. Depot One on the on-time record; Depot Two on late deliveries
E. The two depots are equal on both measures
questions.explanation: On-time percentages are given: Depot One 96%, Depot Two 88%. Late deliveries are the rest: Depot One 168 and Depot Two 108. The depot with the better record still leaves more customers waiting, because it handles more than four times as many deliveries.

questions.prompt:
A class of 40 averages 66 marks. The 15 girls in it average 72.

Select the number of boys AND the mean mark of the boys.
options: E. The boys' mean cannot be worked out from what is given
questions.explanation: There are 40 − 15 = 25 boys. The class scores 2,640 marks in total and the girls 1,080, leaving 1,560 for the boys: 62.4 each. Assuming the class mean sits midway between the two group means gives 60 and ignores that the boys outnumber the girls.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): cases listed — Court P 4,800, Court Q 1,750, Court R 9,600

SOURCE 2 (table): judges sitting — Court P 12, Court Q 5, Court R 26

SOURCE 3 (memo): "The additional judge goes to whichever court carries the most cases for each judge already sitting."

Which court receives the additional judge?
options: D. The three courts are equal
E. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Cases divided by judges: Court P 400, Court Q 350, Court R 369. Court P carries the heaviest load per judge. Court R lists 9,600 cases, twice as many as any other court, but has 26 judges to hear them.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (report): "The ten worst-performing branches were given extra training. Nine of them improved the following quarter."

SOURCE 2 (note): branch results swing widely from quarter to quarter for reasons unconnected with training.

SOURCE 3 (table): of the ten best-performing branches, which received no training, eight did worse the following quarter.

Which statement is best supported?
options: A. The training worked for nine branches in ten
B. The training harmed the best-performing branches
C. Training should in future be given to the best branches instead
D. The sources prove that training has no effect whatever
E. Extreme results tend to drift back towards the middle, so improvement among the worst branches is not evidence that the training worked
questions.explanation: The untrained best branches moved the same way — towards the middle — at almost the same rate, which is what source 2 predicts and what source 3 records. A group picked for being at an extreme will tend to look less extreme next time whatever is done to it. That undercuts the claim the training worked without proving it useless, so the flat denial goes too far.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): annual price — Provider A GBP 3,200.00, Provider B GBP 4,100.00, Provider C GBP 3,750.00

SOURCE 2 (table): delivery format — Provider A XML, Provider B CSV, Provider C CSV

SOURCE 3 (email): "Our system reads CSV only. Buy the cheapest feed we can actually load."

Which provider should be bought?
options: D. All three cost the same
E. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Provider A is cheapest at GBP 3,200.00 but delivers XML, which the system cannot read, so its price is beside the point. Of the two CSV feeds, Provider B at GBP 4,100.00 and Provider C at GBP 3,750.00, Provider C is cheaper by GBP 350.00.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): the fleet covered 1,240,000 km last year.

SOURCE 2 (report): average fuel consumption was 8.5 litres per 100 km.

SOURCE 3 (invoice summary): diesel averaged GBP 1.46 a litre over the year.

What was the fleet's fuel bill for the year?
options: E. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: The fleet burned 1,240,000 × 8.5 / 100 = 105,400 litres, and at GBP 1.46 a litre that comes to GBP 153,884.00. All three sources are needed and each is used once: distance, consumption, price. GBP 105,400.00 is the number of litres read as if it were a bill.

questions.prompt:
Is a quadrilateral a parallelogram?

(1) Both pairs of opposite sides are equal in length.
(2) One pair of opposite angles is equal.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides equal must be a parallelogram, so (1) gives a definite yes. (2) is satisfied by shapes that are not parallelograms — a kite has one pair of opposite angles equal — so it settles nothing on its own.

questions.prompt:
What is the value of xy?

(1) x + y = 10
(2) x − y = 4
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) fits 1 and 9, 5 and 5, and countless other pairs with different products. (2) fits 5 and 1, 7 and 3, and so on. Together they give x = 7 and y = 3, so xy = 21. Two equations are needed for two unknowns, and each statement supplies one.

questions.prompt:
What is the price of one shirt?

(1) Two shirts and a tie cost GBP 74.
(2) A tie costs less than GBP 20.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) leaves two unknowns in one equation: a GBP 14 tie makes the shirts GBP 30 each, while a GBP 4 tie makes them GBP 35. (2) narrows the tie without fixing it, so both of those cases survive. Together the statements still allow a range of shirt prices.

questions.prompt:
How many days did a project run?

(1) It cost GBP 18,000.
(2) It ran from 3 March to 21 March inclusive.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) gives a cost with no daily rate, so the duration could be anything. (2) counts out exactly: from the 3rd to the 21st inclusive is 21 − 3 + 1 = 19 days. Only the second statement bears on the question at all.

questions.prompt:
Which airport handles the most passengers for each runway it has?

Airport | Passengers (millions) | Runways | On time | Staff
Ashford | 4.2 | 1 | 82% | 1,100
Brindley | 18.6 | 2 | 74% | 4,900
Caldwick | 9.4 | 2 | 88% | 2,300
Denby | 27.1 | 3 | 69% | 7,600
Eastmoor | 12.8 | 2 | 91% | 2,900
Fenmarsh | 2.1 | 1 | 94% | 620
questions.explanation: Passengers divided by runways: Ashford 4.2 million, Brindley 9.3 million, Caldwick 4.7 million, Denby 9.03 million, Eastmoor 6.4 million, Fenmarsh 2.1 million. Brindley works its runways hardest at 9.3 million each. Denby carries the most passengers, 27.1 million, but spreads them across 3 runways.

questions.prompt:
Which airport handles the most passengers for each member of staff?

Airport | Passengers (millions) | Runways | On time | Staff
Ashford | 4.2 | 1 | 82% | 1,100
Brindley | 18.6 | 2 | 74% | 4,900
Caldwick | 9.4 | 2 | 88% | 2,300
Denby | 27.1 | 3 | 69% | 7,600
Eastmoor | 12.8 | 2 | 91% | 2,900
Fenmarsh | 2.1 | 1 | 94% | 620
questions.explanation: Passengers divided by staff: Ashford 3,818, Brindley 3,796, Caldwick 4,087, Denby 3,566, Eastmoor 4,414, Fenmarsh 3,387. Eastmoor leads at about 4,414 passengers a head. Denby is much the busiest airport but employs 7,600 people, the largest workforce in the table.

questions.prompt:
How many airports handle more than 10 million passengers and run at 80% on time or better?

Airport | Passengers (millions) | Runways | On time | Staff
Ashford | 4.2 | 1 | 82% | 1,100
Brindley | 18.6 | 2 | 74% | 4,900
Caldwick | 9.4 | 2 | 88% | 2,300
Denby | 27.1 | 3 | 69% | 7,600
Eastmoor | 12.8 | 2 | 91% | 2,900
Fenmarsh | 2.1 | 1 | 94% | 620
questions.explanation: Above 10 million passengers: Brindley 18.6, Denby 27.1, Eastmoor 12.8. At 80% or better: Ashford 82%, Caldwick 88%, Eastmoor 91%, Fenmarsh 94%. Only Eastmoor appears on both lists — 1. Size and punctuality pull against each other everywhere else in the table.

questions.prompt:
How many airports are above the median on punctuality and below the median on passengers?

Airport | Passengers (millions) | Runways | On time | Staff
Ashford | 4.2 | 1 | 82% | 1,100
Brindley | 18.6 | 2 | 74% | 4,900
Caldwick | 9.4 | 2 | 88% | 2,300
Denby | 27.1 | 3 | 69% | 7,600
Eastmoor | 12.8 | 2 | 91% | 2,900
Fenmarsh | 2.1 | 1 | 94% | 620
questions.explanation: The medians are 85% on time and 11.1 million passengers. Above on punctuality: Caldwick, Eastmoor, Fenmarsh. Below on passengers: Ashford, Caldwick, Fenmarsh. On both: Caldwick and Fenmarsh — 2. The quietest airports are mostly the punctual ones, but the smallest of all is not the only one on the list.
